title: Japan and India focus on culture to connect
gist: India has become the world's second-largest anime market after China with roughly 180 million viewers and a projected US$5 billion by 2032, and the Takaichi–Modi summit formally elevated anime, manga, gaming and film to the bilateral agenda. Kodansha is responding to rampant Indian piracy by opening a Mumbai printing house — the first major Japanese comic publisher to localise production in India.

themes.theme: India as the second-largest anime market

insights.claim: India has become the world's second-largest anime market after China this year, with around 180 million viewers.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: A 180-million-viewer market reframes India from a marginal to a top-two territory for Japanese content licensors and streaming platforms.
insights.locator: This year, India's enthusiasm for Japanese entertainment

insights.claim: India's anime market is projected to reach about US$5 billion by 2032.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Sizes a concrete monetisation runway for Japanese IP holders, streaming distributors and merchandise licensors in India.
insights.quote: The country’s anime appetite is set to bulge to about US $5 billion by 2032.
insights.locator: The country's anime appetite is set to bulge

insights.claim: India's first anime and manga school launched last year in Hyderabad as a collaboration between IACG Multimedia College and Kyoto Seika University, building local production capacity rather than only consumption.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Local training pipelines are the precondition for India moving up the animation value chain from audience to outsourced production hub.
insights.locator: Last year, India's first anime and manga school was launched

insights.claim: Kodansha, a major Japanese publisher, is aghast at explosive sales of pirated copies of its comic books in India and will soon open a printing house in Mumbai — the first major Japanese comic book publisher to do so.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Piracy scale is large enough to justify onshore printing capex — a template for other Japanese IP owners entering India, and a watch item for legitimate-format revenue conversion.
insights.locator: Kodansha, a major Japanese publisher – is aghast

insights.claim: The popularity of Japanese comics in India is simultaneously positive and negative for rights holders, because demand is real but a large share of it is being captured by pirated distribution rather than licensed channels.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Headline viewer and market-size numbers overstate realisable revenue until distribution and enforcement are fixed — discount monetisation forecasts accordingly.
insights.locator: This can be positive and negative

insights.claim: At the 16th India-Japan Annual Summit, Prime Ministers Sanae Takaichi and Narendra Modi jointly highlighted "the important role played by creative industries, such as anime, manga, gaming, and films, especially among the youth" alongside the usual defence, technology and supply-chain agreements.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: State-level endorsement of creative industries typically precedes market-access, co-production and IP-enforcement measures — a policy tailwind for content firms.
insights.quote: the important role played by creative industries, such as anime, manga, gaming, and films, especially among the youth
insights.locator: During Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's recent visit to India

insights.claim: Japan and India are celebrating the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations, and both governments have deliberately built cultural consumption into the official relationship rather than treating it as incidental.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Soft-power alignment lowers political friction for Japanese commercial expansion into India across media and consumer sectors.
insights.locator: As Japan and India celebrate the 75th anniversary

themes.theme: How Japan built the soft-power asset

insights.claim: Japanese cultural exports only penetrated Western minds once Japan picked up pace as an economic power in the 1980s, when Sony, Nintendo and Toyota had become global leviathans — economic weight preceded cultural reach.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Implies soft-power monetisation follows hard economic scale, a lens for judging which rising economies' cultural exports are investable next.
insights.locator: Only when Japan picked up pace as an economic power in the 1980s

insights.claim: Japan's Agency of Cultural Affairs began promoting manga, anime and video game exhibitions in 1997, after the Pokémon video game's late-1990s success made the government realise it was sitting on a golden egg.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: State promotion of content industries has a nearly 30-year institutional track record in Japan — durable policy support, not a new initiative.
insights.locator: In the late 1990s, the video game Pokémon arrived

insights.claim: The anime business model historically tested content in cheap print manga first and animated only what clicked, an option-like development pipeline that limited downside on production spend.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Explains the structurally high hit rate of Japanese animated IP versus Western studio models — relevant to comparing content-company economics.
insights.quote: Producers would first try different manga sketches in print. If something clicked, it would be animated.
insights.locator: For anime, popularity increased after the Second World War

insights.claim: Toei Animation pursued becoming the "Disney of the East" by producing animated films for a Western audience, but results were initially humdrum until Japan's economic rise changed reception.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Cultural export success can lag product quality by decades — patience on market entry timing matters more than content strategy alone.
insights.locator: In its quest to become the "Disney of the East"

insights.claim: Donald Trump published a full-page newspaper advertisement criticising allies like Japan for building trade surpluses behind American protection during the 1980s, even as American consumers were becoming hooked on Japanese visual culture.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that trade-friction rhetoric and deepening consumer cultural dependence can run in parallel — relevant to current tariff-era assumptions.
insights.locator: Also, around this time, Donald Trump published a full page advertisement

insights.claim: Japanese cartoons like Naruto and Dragon Ball Z became Indian household staples by the early 2000s, helped by adaptation with local soundtracks and delivered through television as India opened up economically in the late 1990s.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Two decades of localised TV exposure created the installed audience base that today's streaming and merchandise monetisation can harvest.
insights.locator: By the early 2000s, Japanese cartoons like Naruto

insights.claim: Genre breadth is a key driver of manga and anime's resonance — fantasy, science fiction, romance and dark humour give the format audience segments across teenagers, young men and adults simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Broad demographic reach means anime is not a niche youth category, supporting larger addressable-market assumptions for licensors.
insights.quote: From fantasy and science fiction to romance and punchy dark humour, there is something for everyone.
insights.locator: What is it about Japanese manga and anime

insights.claim: Many manga are classic bildungsroman narratives with complex characters that audiences grow up alongside, producing long-duration engagement with single franchises rather than one-off consumption.
insights.speaker: Ved Shinde
insights.so_what: Multi-decade franchise loyalty underpins recurring revenue from long-running IP — the economic reason Japanese content libraries hold value.
insights.quote: One grows up with the lead characters.
insights.locator: Many comics are also classic bildungsroman stories
